articleTitle: Aspects of the design of the James Clerk Maxwell Telescope
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Mechanical Aspects of Antenna Design
abstract: The JCMT (James Clerk Maxwell Telescope) design has been successful in meeting the requirement for extreme accuracy set by the application to submillimetre astronomy. Some of the techniques-the homologous design of the structure, for example, and perhaps the manufacture and adjustment of the panels-are relevant to the design of antennas used in other fields, especially those where high frequencies and large collecting areas are involved.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Mechanical Aspects of Antenna Design
abstract: Describes an innovative satcom antenna for a land-mobile application. It is a low profile design, based on a Luneberg lens and reflector combination, and operates in the microwave X-band. Beam steering and stabilization is achieved through the use of a novel epicyclic gearbox, driven by attitude and heading sensors.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Novel technique for the presentation of antenna reflector deformations under environmental and gravity loads
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Mechanical Aspects of Antenna Design
abstract: Outlines an interesting and useful technique for the display of reflector deformations on large, multi-panelled antennas. Advantages have been demonstrated for this technique, particularly in clarity of presentation of information. The technique has proved beneficial in easing communication between RF and structural/mechanical engineers.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Mechanical Aspects of Antenna Design
abstract: A reflector surface must, by definition, reflect microwave radiation but it must also fulfil a number of other equally important requirements. This paper considers the types of surfaces currently available that meet these requirements and the methods used to produce them. However, there is a great deal of work currently being done developing new types of cost effective reflecting surfaces, primarily for DBS, Receive Only antennas and this work may provide viable alternatives in the near future.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The antenna engineer's requirements for a broadcasting structure
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Mechanical Aspects of Antenna Design
abstract: Discusses some of the conflicting requirements of the antenna designer and the structural engineer which need to be reconciled to give the most cost-effective combination of antenna and support structure for broadcast transmitting systems.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Design of a phased array antenna using solid state transmit/receive modules
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Mechanical Aspects of Antenna Design
abstract: With the maturing of the technology to achieve solid state transmit/receive modules using both gallium arsenide and silicon the possibilities of a solid state phased array antenna is becoming a practical proposition. We have recently seen the progress of the MOD sponsored MESAR demonstrator programme in the UK and a variety of other programmes worldwide. More recently there have been evaluations to enable transmit/receive modules to become affordable and available. This paper presents some of the trade-offs and design decisions that have been implemented to support these requirements. The design of the antenna has included the thermal aspects, weight considerations and mechanical construction.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Cost-effective mechanical design associated with low quantity production
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Mechanical Aspects of Antenna Design
abstract: On low quantity production, constraints are based around development monies and because the designer is prevented from adopting the feasibility study, prototype, production route of a development program the ultimate design will be right rather than optimum. the control of the costs of the system rest with close liaison between the engineers with a mutual understanding of each others problems and a commitment to the projects success, rather than the success of any particular aspect to the detriment of others. In the particular example used, the mechanical design of the frame was based upon the understanding that the dish weight and pannier weight was not frozen so the author assumed a heavier weight than was forecast so that the design would be finalised within the project programme with no extra costs. This approach was adopted throughout the project.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Large reflecting zone plates for satellite signal reception
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Mechanical Aspects of Antenna Design
abstract: The principle of the Fresnel zone plate has been well known for over 100 years and applied over the electromagnetic spectrum from millimetre wavelengths to X-rays. Its microwave possibilities, however, appear to have received little attention before 1962, when Van Buskirk and Hendrix proposed its use for satellite communications and as an inexpensive means of making large radio telescopes. All the work referenced is based on circular zone patterns, but it was pointed out to the author by K. Milne that the technique could equally be employed when the circles were projected into any plane arbitrarily inclined to the line-of-sight to the source, thus giving a set of ellipses. This is particularly useful for satellite reception since it provides an antenna which can be mounted vertically on a wall or window, on a sloping or flat roof, or on the ground.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Mechanical implications of higher frequency working in satellite communication ground based antenna systems
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Mechanical Aspects of Antenna Design
abstract: Mechanical design and manufacturing techniques, appropriate to C-Band working have been successfully developed and refined over the years. But these techniques are questionable when applied to Ku-Band working, and are more often than not totally inappropriate for Ka-Band systems. Inevitably the designer is faced with the requirement for greater accuracy of reflector surface. This increase in accuracy combined with the need for greater care in selection of materials and the tighter budget allowable for environment distortion more than offsets the advantages gained by reduction in size. This is particularly true when dealing with combined transmit and receive systems.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Recent developments in carbon fibre reinforced composite mouldings with improved surface profile
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Mechanical Aspects of Antenna Design
abstract: Composite structures can offer performance benefits over traditional materials. Over the last twenty years various products in industries of extreme diversity have evolved incorporating advanced composite mouldings for improved stiffness and weight saving. Particular composite systems providing specific and often unique properties have also enabled technical progress in such as the avionics, cryogenics, medical, sub-sea and communication markets: many examples could be cited. The author looks at lightweight antenna reflector design.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Deflection criteria for microwave antenna support structures: digital radio systems
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Mechanical Aspects of Antenna Design
abstract: Describes the effects of structural movements under wind loads on the performance of terrestrial microwave links and gives guidance on maximum acceptable design deflections. The random movements of structures under wind loads are compared to the antenna performance and the effects of any losses of signal on the system performance. These losses are compared to the CCIR Recommendations for analogue and digital radio links and with British Telecom's operating experience with losses from all causes. Although this will vary with the system used, well designed digital and analogue radio links are found to be almost equally sensitive to information losses due to wind deflection. Suitable deflection criteria are suggested.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The mechanical design and manufacture of a high performance airborne radar antenna
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Mechanical Aspects of Antenna Design
abstract: Outlines the electrical and mechanical requirements imposed on the antenna of a high performance airborne radar. The planar array used to achieve the performance is described briefly and the mechanical design and method of manufacture used to realise it outlined.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>
